summary: Describes the format of files holding messages that have been encrypted or signed with PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), so different programs can read each other's output. It is informational, not a standard, and it was replaced by RFC 4880.

eli5.summary: PGP puts your letter in a locked box and signs it. This note explains how to build the box so anyone with the right key can open it.

questions: what is the pgp message format
subtitle: The packet-based structure for encrypted and signed messages

tldr.problem: PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) provided encryption and digital signatures for email, but implementers needed a standard way to encode these messages so different PGP programs could read each other's output.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1991 defines the format of PGP messages as sequences of typed packets: literal data packets hold the message itself, signature packets provide digital signatures, encrypted-data packets hold ciphertexts, and public-key packets distribute keys. Different packets are layered and composed to create signed, encrypted, or both signed-and-encrypted messages.
tldr.outcome: This specification enabled interoperability between PGP implementations but was eventually superseded by RFC 4880, which defines the OpenPGP format with additional cryptographic algorithms and features.

today: RFC 1991 was a landmark documentation of an already-popular encryption system. The format was obsoleted by RFC 4880, which defines the OpenPGP format with support for additional algorithms (DSA, ElGamal, SHA-1, AES) and extended features. PGP and its descendants (GPG) remain in use for email security and code signing, though adoption of the OpenPGP RFC standard is now widespread.

sections.title: What Is PGP and Why Format Matters
sections.content:
PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) is a system that combines public-key cryptography and conventional encryption to provide confidentiality and digital signatures for electronic mail. Created by Philip Zimmermann in 1991, PGP became widely used despite export restrictions on cryptography. RFC 1991 documents the message format used by PGP versions 2.6 and 2.7, specifying how messages are structured as sequences of labeled packets so that different software implementations can read each other's output.

The problem solved by a standard format is simple: if Alice encrypts a message with one PGP implementation and sends it to Bob who uses a different implementation, Bob's software must be able to read Alice's bytes correctly. Without a published format, this interoperability would be impossible. The RFC defines the serialization format—how to turn abstract concepts like 'a signature' and 'encrypted data' into sequences of bytes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a locked box with a note attached. Different companies build similar boxes, but Alice's box brand must produce boxes that Bob's box brand can open. This document is the instruction manual for how all boxes should look on the inside.

sections.title: Four Layers of Protection and Processing
sections.content:
PGP messages are built from four composable services: digital signature, confidentiality, compression, and ASCII Armor (radix-64 conversion).

Digital signature takes a message, computes a cryptographic hash, and encrypts that hash with the sender's private key. The receiver can decrypt with the sender's public key to verify the message was not altered and came from the claimed sender. Confidentiality works differently: the sender generates a random 128-bit session key, encrypts the message with it using conventional encryption (like IDEA), then encrypts the session key itself with the recipient's public key. Only the recipient can decrypt the session key and read the message. Compression (usually ZIP) happens after signatures but before encryption to reduce message size. Finally, ASCII Armor converts binary output to base-64 text so encrypted messages can transit email systems safely. The RFC emphasizes that these four operations can be applied in combination: sign-then-encrypt is the normal path for messages meant to be confidential.
sections.eli5: Signing writes your name in permanent ink; encryption locks the message in a box; compression squeezes the box smaller; ASCII Armor wraps it in paper that email can handle. You do them in order: sign first (so the signature covers the real message), then encrypt (so the signature is secret), then compress and wrap.

sections.title: Packets: The Basic Building Block
sections.content:
All PGP messages are sequences of packets. Each packet is a labeled container with a header and body. The header is a Cipher Type Byte (CTB) that encodes the packet type (13 types defined) and the length of the packet body. The length can be 1, 2, 4, or unlimited bytes depending on a 2-bit field in the CTB.

PGP defines seven main packet types: literal data packets contain the actual message bytes; signature packets hold the encrypted hash and metadata about the signature; compressed data packets wrap another packet that was compressed; conventional-key-encrypted data packets contain a message encrypted with a one-time session key; public-key-encrypted packets wrap a session key encrypted with a recipient's public key; public-key packets distribute RSA keys; and user ID packets attach names and email addresses to keys. Each packet type has a well-defined binary format with mandatory and optional fields.
sections.eli5: Think of packets like envelopes. Each envelope has a label on the front (the CTB) that says 'this is a message,' 'this is a signature,' or 'this is encrypted.' The receiver reads the label first, then knows how to interpret the bytes inside.

sections.title: Assembling Encrypted and Signed Messages
sections.content:
A signed message requires two packets: a literal data packet (the message) followed by a signature packet. The signature's hash input includes only the literal data bytes, not the literal packet headers, so that detached signatures (stored in separate files) are byte-for-byte identical to attached signatures.

A confidential message adds encryption and optionally compression. By default, PGP compresses the message-plus-signature block with ZIP, wrapping it in a compressed data packet. The compression algorithm (or no compression) is specified by a single byte in the packet. Next, the compressed block is encrypted with a random 128-bit session key using conventional encryption (IDEA), creating a conventional-key-encrypted data packet. That session key is encrypted with the recipient's public key(s) and wrapped in a public-key-encrypted packet that precedes the encrypted data. The public-key-encrypted packet also stores an 8-byte ID derived from the recipient's public key, so the recipient knows which of their keys to try for decryption. A message to multiple recipients has multiple public-key-encrypted packets, one for each key ID, all preceding the single encrypted data block.
sections.eli5: To send a secret signed letter: first write the letter (literal packet), sign it (signature packet), compress both (compressed packet), encrypt with a new key (encrypted packet), then send that key to each recipient encrypted with their public key (public-key-encrypted packets). The encrypted key goes first; the encrypted message follows.

sections.title: Distributing Public Keys
sections.content: Public keys are exchanged as transferable public keys, which are sequences of three packet types: a public-key packet containing the RSA modulus and encryption exponent, one or more user ID packets naming the key owner, and zero or more signature packets certifying the key. User ID packets are usually formatted as 'Name (comment) email-address', so keys are human-readable. Signature packets follow the user IDs they certify—multiple people can sign a key to vouch that it really belongs to the claimed person. The RFC specifies signature types to distinguish 'I wrote this document' from 'I certify this key belongs to Alice' and various levels of certification confidence. This packet structure enables key servers to distribute and certify keys without understanding the mathematics of RSA.
sections.eli5: A public key is like a business card. It shows the person's name and email, but it can also have signatures from other people saying 'I checked, this is really Alice's key.' Each signature is a packet appended to the card.
